Anthropic filed its S-1 publicly today. This note walks through the filing,
and at the end we include the Anthropic financial model we built off it. The
model rests only on the S-1 and prior public information, so a number of
inputs are still open and we will keep refining it. Please contact
[Sales@Funda.ai](https://substack.com/redirect/b9886348-dbd1-4b70-a723-c69ae1725186?j=eyJ1IjoiNTBkYXR1In0.wMhVDxPSNfOaCS4gLOy6QmLs4ijRPD8hP3NmO4HbRXc)
to learn more about the EPS model.

**What we focused on:**

  * Revenue and margins: 2Q26 revenue of $11.6bn at a 19% non-GAAP operating margin; 11% for the first nine months

  * How and when ~$800bn of compute commitments flow into costs

  * Whether the cash covers it: ~$132bn on the balance sheet; with IPO proceeds, the model trough is ~$150bn

  * Demand and customer mix: NRR of ~900%; top five customers ~25% of revenue

  * What it means for the AI narrative, and the numbers to watch before the IPO

  * How we built the EPS model

### **I. Revenue**

#### **1\. Quarterly Revenue**

Quarterly revenue went $376M, $787M, $1.38bn, $2.04bn, $4.73bn and $11.56bn
from 1Q25 to 2Q26. 2Q26 was up 1,368% y/y, while compute and infrastructure
expense grew only 300%.

|
[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LXr6!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe921f27f-3d84-4024-86e0-d2d130fc51bb_2000x1120.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/a5903cb4-1f4c-4e1c-9777-a06517aaf2a9?j=eyJ1IjoiNTBkYXR1In0.wMhVDxPSNfOaCS4gLOy6QmLs4ijRPD8hP3NmO4HbRXc)|  
---|---|---  
  
_Source: Anthropic S-1, FUNDA analysis_

#### **2\. 3Q is blank, but you can back into it**

The S-1 leaves 3Q26 revenue blank, but elsewhere states that 3Q26 revenue was
86x 4Q24. With 4Q24 at $197M, that implies ~$16.9bn for 3Q26, in line with the
$16.8bn disclosed at the October investor day. Two other data points get you
to the same place: TTM revenue up ~1,200% y/y, and TTM revenue per employee
above $6.6M on ~5,300 employees.

#### **3\. Almost all revenue comes from new models**

Model versions released in the six months to September 30 drove more than 80%
of 3Q revenue. Older models get replaced very quickly.

#### **4\. Consumption is the bulk of it**

Consumption-based revenue was 75% of the total in 2024, 83% in 2025 and 80% in
1H26; the rest is subscriptions.

|

---|---|---  
  
_Source: Anthropic S-1, FUNDA analysis_

### **II. Run-rate revenue and revenue recognition**

#### **1\. How run-rate is defined**

The S-1 defines Run-Rate Revenue as trailing-28-day consumption revenue x 13
plus monthly subscription revenue x 12. The company attaches three caveats:

  * it includes customers later found to have violated the usage policy;

  * it is seasonal, with usage dipping over the summer and winter holidays;

  * growth is expected to slow.

#### **2\. Revenue is booked gross**

When customers buy Claude through the AWS, GCP or Azure marketplaces,
Anthropic is the principal and books the full amount as revenue; the cloud
providers’ cut sits in “sales, marketing and partnerships.” Marketplace
revenue rose from 11% of the total in 2023 to 32% in 2024, 47% in 2025 and 48%
in 1H26. Adjust for this before comparing multiples with companies that report
net.

|
[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wS9v!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F183b801a-3ca8-422f-8594-6fc216b01ef4_2000x1120.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/7b9026a0-46b5-4ea7-8918-4eab8e409ae4?j=eyJ1IjoiNTBkYXR1In0.wMhVDxPSNfOaCS4gLOy6QmLs4ijRPD8hP3NmO4HbRXc)|  
---|---|---  
  
_Source: Anthropic S-1, FUNDA analysis_

#### **3\. Distillation revenue is now quantified**

The S-1 states:

> “we estimate that revenue from such customers represented approximately 5%
> to 7% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026”

“Such customers” are those that violated the usage policy or commercial terms.
On ~$33bn of 9M26 revenue, that is roughly $1.7–2.3bn (our estimate).
Enforcement was stepped up in August–September, so the share should come down.

#### **4\. The holiday effect is real**

Total customer spend in the two weeks to January 2, 2026 was ~20% below the
prior two weeks. Any run-rate struck off the last week of December will be
depressed by the holidays.

#### **5\. Some numbers are left blank on purpose**

Run-Rate Revenue as of October 31, 3Q revenue, liquidity at September 30,
total compute commitments and the price range are all blank. We expect them in
the S-1/A.

### **III. Margins (non-GAAP)**

#### **1\. Gross margin is in the footnotes**

From 2025 the P&L presents expenses by nature, so there is no gross profit
line. Note 8 still breaks costs out by function, and cost of revenue is
“substantially all” compute and infrastructure for serving customer workloads.
The implied gross margin: −95% in 2024, 40% in 2025, 12% in 1H25 and 85% in
1H26.

85% flatters the picture: the cloud providers’ revenue share and inference for
free users both sit in sales and marketing, not cost of revenue.

|
[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SHLF!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F94d649f8-8150-4ad0-b0ee-c7ce89ab130b_2000x1120.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/481bea1a-aa78-4e29-a11b-543aed347183?j=eyJ1IjoiNTBkYXR1In0.wMhVDxPSNfOaCS4gLOy6QmLs4ijRPD8hP3NmO4HbRXc)|  
---|---|---  
  
_Source: Anthropic S-1 (Note 8), FUNDA estimates_

#### **2\. Compute intensity is falling fast**

Compute and infrastructure expense (serving, training, research and internal
use) as a share of revenue: 251% in 1Q25 and 144% in 4Q25; 72% in 1Q26 and 48%
in 2Q26.

|
[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uM5Q!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4cfed473-83d2-4e77-95a0-ad47220b47ff_2000x1120.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/38d46ceb-3df7-43d0-86e8-a0eb5cadd3e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNTBkYXR1In0.wMhVDxPSNfOaCS4gLOy6QmLs4ijRPD8hP3NmO4HbRXc)|  
---|---|---  
  
_Source: Anthropic S-1, FUNDA analysis_

#### **3\. 2Q26 cost structure**

Excluding SBC: compute 48% of revenue, sales, marketing and partnerships 18.5%
(including the cloud providers’ share), other operating ~9% and personnel ~5%.
SBC was $1.26bn, ~11% of revenue.

|
[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xBNj!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa0569b29-44f4-4a08-b707-e66d049769e7_2000x1120.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/c21c5d3c-57ce-493a-871e-3f72c8d5d44f?j=eyJ1IjoiNTBkYXR1In0.wMhVDxPSNfOaCS4gLOy6QmLs4ijRPD8hP3NmO4HbRXc)|  
---|---|---  
  
_Source: Anthropic S-1, FUNDA analysis_

#### **4\. Non-GAAP operating margin**

Annual: −1,273% in 2023, −722% in 2024 and −106% in 2025; +10% in 1H26
($1.6bn). The S-1 also gives the quarters: −221%, −129%, −93% and −84% through
2025, then −13% in 1Q26 and +19% in 2Q26. 2Q26 adjusted operating income of
$2.24bn is GAAP operating income of $0.97bn plus $1.26bn of SBC.

#### **5\. 3Q likely back to ~12%**

At the October 14 investor meeting, the company put the adjusted operating
margin for the year through 3Q at 11%. The Information later corrected this to
a nine-month figure, not 3Q alone; Bloomberg said “over 11%.” That implies
~$2.0bn of adjusted operating income in 3Q, a ~12% margin, about 7 points
below 2Q.

We see 2Q’s 19% as a high-water mark. Revenue rose 144% q/q in 2Q while
compute is locked in 12–18 months ahead, so compute fell from 72% to 48% of
revenue: revenue simply outran capacity. As new capacity came on in 3Q (Google
from April, Amazon from May, SpaceXAI ramping into year-end), plus the pricier
short-term compute the S-1 flags, margins settled back around 12%. The
sustainable level looks closer to 3Q than 2Q.

|

### **IV. Margins will stay volatile,**

#### **1\. Why**

Compute is contracted 12–18 months ahead and starts hitting the P&L as soon as
capacity comes online, in large blocks and ahead of the revenue it will
support. The S-1 notes that margins expanded sharply y/y over the first nine
months, but expects them to compress while large amounts of new capacity come
on, and to swing meaningfully even as the underlying economics improve.

#### **2\. The path in our model**

Adjusted operating margin of ~12% in 3Q26, ~−9% in 4Q26 and ~−22% in 1Q27,
narrowing from there. On a full-year basis: ~−13% in 2027, ~−4% in 2028, back
to ~14% in 2029 and ~26% in 2030. The driver is the wave of contracted
capacity landing in 2027–28, with costs running ahead of revenue (see Section
VI).

#### **3\. Short-term compute is the near-term squeeze**

When demand exceeds long-term contracted capacity, Anthropic buys short-term
compute at a higher unit cost. The S-1 expects to lean on short-term compute
more in the near term, which will weigh on margins.

#### **4\. Compute could get more expensive**

The S-1 warns compute costs could rise materially, especially if AI demand
accelerates or the ability to train frontier models spreads and competition
shifts to securing compute. It lists factors largely outside its control:
concentrated chip and memory supply, tight power and data-center capacity, and
export controls.

#### **5\. The response: “Anthropic Direct”**

The company is moving from cloud-only contracts to a hybrid model: leasing
chips directly and placing them in dedicated facilities run by third parties.
Data centers take longer to build but are a small share of total cost, so it
locks in the sites first and pushes the much larger accelerator commitments
later. Once that capacity is live, cheap long-term compute can replace
expensive short-term compute.

#### **6\. Pricing to customers keeps falling**

Opus 5.5 costs ~40% less per task than Opus 5; Fable 5.1 is ~25% cheaper than
Fable 5 on standard workloads and up to 45% cheaper on complex coding and
agentic tasks. The S-1’s argument is that compute efficiency is what lets it
cut prices and hold margins.

### **VI. Cash and funding: can they pay for it?**

#### **1\. What they raised, and what is left**

From 2023 through 1H26, Anthropic raised ~$140bn in cash (preferred stock,
convertible notes and SAFEs), $110bn of it in 1H26 alone, including the
$65.2bn Series H. At June 30 it held $112.4bn of cash and equivalents plus

restricted cash.

#### **2\. Undrawn capacity**

A $15bn revolver (upsized in September, undrawn) and up to $77bn of partner
note facilities: Google $20bn, Amazon $15bn (tied to compute-delivery

proceeds in the model (4Q26).

#### **3\. Against the megacaps**

Cash and liquid investments at June 30 (gross of debt): Alphabet $242bn,
Anthropic $132bn, Amazon $123bn, Meta $90bn, Microsoft $77bn, Tencent ~$75bn,
Alibaba ~$70bn. Anthropic holds more cash than Amazon, Meta or Microsoft, yet
the SpaceXAI contract alone runs ~$37bn a year from December 2026.

### **VII. How Anthropic gets TPUs, and who books the revenue**

#### **1\. GOOG and Broadcom**

One is renting from Google Cloud: at least ~$114.5bn from April 2026 to July
2033, take-or-pay. The other is leasing TPU-based systems from Broadcom under
five-year master equipment leases: ~$161.2bn of rent, of which the 2026 Lease
Arrangement is ~$125.2bn. The TPUs are leased, not bought, but they are
accounted for as finance leases and sit on the balance sheet, and the S-1
mentions an early buyout option.

#### **2\. How the rent is paid**

Rent is paid quarterly once the equipment is ready for service. The leases sit
in two special-purpose subsidiaries, guaranteed by Anthropic PBC and secured
by the equipment. If needed, Anthropic can fund rent by issuing up to $42bn of
convertible notes to Broadcom, settled in Class N shares.

#### **3\. The data centers aren’t Anthropic’s**

The hardware sits in dedicated facilities operated by others, with Fluidstack,
for example, providing colocation and services. Anthropic has also given
developers guarantees and cost-reimbursement arrangements, with a maximum
potential payment of ~$0.8bn at June 30.

#### **4\. Who books the revenue (Our view)**

On the GCP route, Anthropic is a Google Cloud customer: this is Google Cloud
revenue and sits in the Cloud backlog ($513.9bn at June 30). On the Broadcom
route, the lessor is Broadcom, not Google; a finance lease for the lessee
usually means a sales-type lease for the lessor, with revenue recognized
upfront when the equipment is ready for service. Our current view is that
Google books its TPU sales to Broadcom gross, without netting Broadcom’s cost,
though net treatment cannot be ruled out. The S-1 adds nothing further.

### **IX. Models and training**

#### **1\. Pre-training is run like a capital budget**

Improvements are tested at small scale and have to hold up at scale before
they go into a frontier run. The S-1 calls frontier runs “planned, scheduled
capital deployments.”

#### **2\. Post-training matters more and more**

With the shift from assistants to agents, most of what makes a model useful,
accurate and safe now happens in post-training. Agentic skills such as coding,
tool use and operating on a user’s behalf are also trained at this stage, on
complete, realistic tasks.

#### **3\. Beyond scaling laws**

Four of the co-founders were lead authors on the original scaling-laws paper.
The company says proprietary “compute multipliers” from pre- and post-training
research let it improve faster than scaling laws alone would, while inference
engineering keeps pushing serving compute down. The risk factors also flag
that scaling laws could plateau.

#### **4\. What each generation brings**

Deeper reasoning, longer autonomous work and more complex tasks. On one
internal benchmark, the success rate reached ~90% in September 2026, up ~50
points in nine months. Training costs are not disclosed: the S-1 says only
that frontier runs take weeks to months, cost at least several million
dollars, and have sometimes failed or underperformed. What it does disclose is
that price per task has fallen with every release.

#### **5\. Returns**

Revenue has grown far faster than compute expense, and new models earn back
most of their investment within a few quarters. The flip side: revenue from
older models decays quickly, which forces continuous investment in the newest,
most compute-hungry models. R&D was ~60% of 1H26 revenue.

#### **6\. Where the data comes from**

Public web data (crawled pages, scanned books), licensed or custom third-party
datasets, and synthetic data generated by its own models. The company says it
respects robots.txt, paywalls and login gates, but concedes it may not always
succeed. The $1.5bn Bartz settlement was approved in July 2026. A large share
of customer traffic is covered by zero-data-retention terms.

#### **7\. Constitutional training and safety**

Claude is trained against a published constitution with four priorities:
broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with guidelines, and genuinely
helpful. One interesting detail: training on constitution-style documents
alongside fictional stories about well-aligned AI reduces Claude’s
misalignment rate.

Safety can also slow the roadmap. Anthropic once delayed pre-training of a new
frontier base model by more than a month to harden protections against weight
theft. In 2026, during pre-release cyber evaluations, a model accessed real
computer systems without authorization; the company paused some evaluations
and higher-risk RL environments in response.

### **X. How the founders see the future**

A founders’ letter is unusual in an IPO filing. A few passages stood out to
us.

#### **1\. Reinvent rather than defend**

> “We will be constantly seeking to reinvent our business, releasing new
> classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing
> ones.”

In plain terms: less energy spent protecting today’s products and business
model, more on building new categories.

#### **2\. The timeline for viable AI**

> “AI chatbots became viable around 2022, and AI coding agents around 2025; AI
> agents for general knowledge work and scientific discovery are gradually
> becoming viable in 2026.”

Claude Cowork extends Claude Code’s agent architecture to every knowledge
worker.

#### **3\. How big the market is**

  * Global knowledge work worth more than $40tn in 2025 (company estimate);

  * More than 1bn knowledge workers by 2028 (IDC);

  * $22.5tn of cumulative economic impact from AI by 2031 (IDC);

  * Pharma spend alone above $2tn in 2026.

#### **4\. “A country of geniuses in a datacenter”**

Anthropic expects “powerful AI” to be broadly available within a few years.
Its definition: expert-level performance in most fields, the ability to use
any interface a human can, to work autonomously for hours to weeks, to
coordinate across many instances, and to operate lab equipment and robots.

#### **5\. Why the compute bets look so large**

The founders say forward investments can look irresponsibly large at first
glance because AI’s value sits on an exponential curve. Their analogy is
pharma R&D, only faster and bigger. The hedge is to trade some upside for
downside protection: reselling surplus compute, improving efficiency, raising
capital.

#### **6\. Revenue they chose to leave on the table**

Claude carries no ads. Claude Mythos Preview was not broadly released because
of cybersecurity risk and later shipped as Fable 5, forgoing meaningful
revenue; the company also gave cyber defenders ~$100M of usage credits. If
needed, they may slow capability progress for safety, even at a competitive
cost.

#### **7\. The historical reference they chose**

From 2000 to 2025, revenue at the world’s ten largest tech companies grew
~38x, roughly 11x the pace of global GDP. The founders argue the exponential
in machine cognition will matter far more than Moore’s Law.

#### **8\. On investor expectations**

The founders pass on advice from several entrepreneurs who had been through an
IPO:

> “never let your company be worth a dollar more than it is actually worth”

Their own rule: under-promise and over-deliver.

### **XI. Dilution and lock-ups**

  * **$77bn of convertible note capacity:** Google $20bn, Amazon $15bn and Broadcom $42bn, converting at a trailing volume-weighted average price;

  * **Google’s IPO purchase right:** up to $10bn of additional stock at the IPO price;

  * **Public Benefit Fund:** 5% of fully diluted shares, plus up to 2% more for every 50% rise in the share price;

  * **Staggered lock-up releases:** tranches on day one and on days 27, 48, 62 and 76; roughly every two weeks after FY2026 results; the 180-day group is fully released at 1Q27 results or day 180. The 365-day group (including all seven co-founders) is released in stages through 3Q27 results;

  * **Founders’ pledge:** each co-founder has pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a voluntary and revocable commitment.

#### **1\. The positives**

  * **Scale.** Disclosed compute commitments total ~$780–810bn. In our model, contracted capacity cost is ~$98.6bn in 2027, ~$152.3bn in 2028 and ~$182.0bn in 2029, 4–8x the 2Q26 annualized compute expense (~$22.2bn).

  * **Demand exceeds supply.** The S-1 says it buys pricier short-term compute when long-term capacity falls short, and expects short-term usage to rise near term. Compute is still a sellers’ market.

  * **Frontier training cannot stop.** More than 80% of 3Q revenue came from models released within six months, older-model revenue decays fast, and the company has to keep training the newest, most compute-hungry models.

  * **They can pay.** A 19% non-GAAP operating margin in 2Q, ~$132bn of cash at June 30, plus ~$60bn of IPO proceeds (our assumption). In our base case, cash and short-term investments bottom at ~$150.1bn (end-2028) and rebuild on operating cash flow. Counterparty risk is lower than the market fears, and the more cash Anthropic generates, the more compute it will be willing to sign.

#### **2\. The negatives**

  * **Compute per dollar of revenue is falling.** Price per task drops 25–45% with each generation (Opus 5.5 ~40% below Opus 5; Fable 5.1 25% lower, up to 45% on complex tasks). Compute multipliers and inference engineering keep pushing serving compute down.

  * **Growth will slow.** The S-1 says plainly that revenue growth will decline, possibly sharply and faster than expected, and that seasonality will become more visible as it does.

  * **The commitments are softer than they look.** The $120.5bn SpaceXAI figure is a ceiling and can be cancelled on 90 days’ notice after January and March 2027; Nscale and Lambda bill only on delivery and depend on the counterparties’ financing and sites (the $34.9bn Lambda deal can be terminated if sites are not secured); AMD and the TPU add-on have no fixed amounts. What is truly non-cancellable is mainly Broadcom, Google, Amazon and Microsoft.

  * **Anthropic could become a seller of compute.** The founders list reselling surplus compute as downside protection. If demand disappoints, that capacity comes back to the market.

  * **Margin pressure will push down prices.** Margins went from 19% in 2Q to ~12% in 3Q, which the S-1 ties to expensive short-term compute. Anthropic Direct exists to lower unit compute cost, which is negative for cloud and neocloud margins and, over time, for chip pricing (our view).

  * **The mix tilts toward ASICs.** TPU-related commitments (Broadcom + Google) exceed $400bn, versus ~$206bn tied to NVIDIA, most of it through neoclouds.

  * **Tail risk.** Revenue is usage-based, compute is take-or-pay, and the agreements are cross-defaulted. In our downside case (end-2027 run-rate of ~$109bn, growth below 30% thereafter) the IPO proceeds just about carry it, with cash bottoming at ~$15bn; if the run-rate stalls at ~$83bn, cash turns negative in 2029. At that point the Broadcom leases and neocloud contracts become counterparty risk.

### **XIII. What to watch before the IPO**

  * **October 31 run-rate (the big one).** Blank in the S-1. Whether Opus 5.5 moved October ARR is the single most important near-term valuation driver.

  * **Full 3Q financials.** Under the SEC staleness rule (Reg S-X 3-12), the June 30 financials go stale around mid-November. If the IPO lands before Thanksgiving as reported, the S-1/A will likely need financials through September 30: 3Q revenue, 3Q adjusted operating margin (testing the 11% for 9M and ~12% for 3Q), compute as a share of revenue, and cash flow.

  * **Distillation share and December seasonality.** Whether revenue from policy violators falls to a negligible level in 4Q; the drop in usage over the last two weeks of December feeds directly into the year-end exit run-rate.

  * **New models and price cuts.** Whether a new generation ships before the IPO, and how far price per task falls again. Both drive revenue growth and compute per unit.

  * **Lock-up percentages.** The share released in each tranche is still blank, and it sets the supply overhang in the first months after listing.

### **XIV. Model update: Anthropic EPS model (first cut)**

This is a first-cut model built on October 26, the day the S-1 went public,
using only the S-1 and a handful of public reports. Plenty is still
unresolved, above all how the compute commitments flow into costs. We will
keep refining it as the S-1/A, quarterly results and channel checks come in,
and the numbers will move.
